doc.title: Nick Brignola interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, July 28, 1997

title: Fitting in at jazz parties: the 'character actor' approach
summary: He explains the repertoire and attitude needed at jazz parties, with a famous alto player's advice that a party is a holiday.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Playing for the audience: communicating from the bandstand

blocks.x: You know if a musician today wanted to get into that circuit, what do they have to — besides that they have to play good — but is there other things? I mean like there’s a standard repertory that you have.

You just better know a lot of tunes from the ‘20s right up to the ‘50s, and you better be able to put your ego at the door and be able to fit in. I always looked at it as being a great character actor. You know if you’re an actor on a stage, you can’t go in there being the big star. But if you’re a great character actor and somebody says, “Okay, at two o’clock you’re going to be in this band,” like Jay McShann’s playing piano, Ray Brown’s playing drums, Phil Woods playing alto, and Bob Wilber’s playing clarinet. You know all of a sudden you’re saying, “Wait a minute. What are we going to play?” Well we’ll tell you that when you get there, but you better be ready to play this role. And I think the more you can do that, the more success you have. I used to see musicians come in like they’re going to do their thing. And they weren’t back there the next time. So I mean there’s a point to where you’ve got to be one of the crowd. And it’s fun. I won’t mention any names, but a musician, when I first did one of these parties I was very disappointed because I was kind of with that head, “I’m going to go in and play what I do best, and I’m going to try to be as good as I can.” And then I realized that they were just cutting my legs off. They were putting me in positions and putting me with musicians that wouldn’t allow me to do what I — so I was kind of depressed and I was sitting there, and this guy, a famous alto player, said to me, “Cheer up,” he says, “where else could you be with all these great musicians. It’s a holiday.” He says, “Look at it this way: it’s nice to have a gig once a year that has nothing to do with music” which I thought was a great line. And you might — I’ll tell you later who said that, but you probably know already.

But after I heard that it put everything in perspective and I laughed, and I was able to laugh at that point, and I said you know, he’s right. Not that you shouldn’t get up and play as good as you can, but don’t take it so seriously, and just enjoy the situation.
Well there’s an art to that too — playing within the correct context.
